## Preparing environment

```{r}
library(tidyverse)
library(dplyr)
library(tidyr)
library(purrr)
library(stringr)
library(ggplot2)
library(readr)
library(tibble)
library(gridExtra)
```
## Loading lcms data

```{r}
lcms_data <- read_tsv("MSdata_ST000355_AN000581.txt", col_names = TRUE, show_col_types = TRUE)

lcms_data
```

## Separating sample metadata (Diagnosis, Stage) from the metabolite matrix

The "Factors" row packs `Diagnosis` and `Stage` into a single string per sample
(e.g. `Diagnosis:Breast cancer | Stage:1`). Pull it into its own metadata table, then drop it from `lcms_data` so the remaining rows are all metabolite abundances.

```{r}
sample_metadata <- lcms_data |>
  filter(Samples == "Factors") |>
  select(-Samples) |>
  pivot_longer(everything(), names_to = "sample_id", values_to = "factor_string") |>
  mutate(
    Diagnosis = str_extract(factor_string, "(?<=Diagnosis:)[^|]+") |> str_trim(),
    Stage     = str_extract(factor_string, "(?<=Stage:)[^|]+") |> str_trim()
  ) |>
  select(sample_id, Diagnosis, Stage)

lcms_data_abundances <- lcms_data |>
  filter(Samples != "Factors") |>
  rename(Compound = Samples)

sample_metadata
sample_metadata |> 
  count(Stage) |> print()
lcms_data_abundances
```

## Cross-checking against metadata.csv

`metadata.csv` provides Diagnosis/Stage independently (via `Sample name`).
Join it to `sample_metadata` and check agreement.

```{r}
metadata_csv <- read_csv("metadata.csv", show_col_types = FALSE)
metadata_csv

metadata_merged <- sample_metadata |>
  inner_join(metadata_csv, by = c("sample_id" = "Sample name")) |>
  mutate(
    diagnosis_match = Diagnosis.x == Diagnosis.y,
    stage_match = as.character(Stage.x) == as.character(Stage.y)
  )

nrow(sample_metadata)
nrow(metadata_csv)
nrow(metadata_merged)

metadata_merged |> count(diagnosis_match)
metadata_merged |> count(stage_match)
metadata_merged
View(metadata_merged)
```


## polishing merged metadata

```{r}
metadata_merged <- 
  metadata_merged |> 
  rename(Stage = Stage.x, Diagnosis = Diagnosis.x) |> 
  select(-ends_with(c(".y", "_match")), -`Subject name`, -`Sample_Data:Sub-group`)

metadata_merged$Stage <- as.factor(metadata_merged$Stage)
metadata_merged
```




## Long-format metabolite table for exploratory plots

Pivot `lcms_data_abundances` into long format (one row per compound × sample)
and join with `metadata_merged` so Diagnosis/Stage are available for plotting.

```{r}
lcms_long <- lcms_data_abundances |>
  pivot_longer(-Compound, names_to = "sample_id", values_to = "abundance") |>
  mutate(abundance = as.numeric(abundance)) |>
  left_join(metadata_merged, by = "sample_id")
lcms_long

# 146 of ~20,900 compound x sample values are missing in the source data
sum(is.na(lcms_long$abundance))
lcms_long
```

## Heatmap of metabolite abundances by Stage

Mean abundance per compound is computed for each Stage, then z-scored within each compound (row) so all 99 compounds — despite very different absolute scales — are visually comparable. Compounds are ordered by hierarchical clustering to group similar Stage-response patterns together.

```{r, fig.height=14}
heatmap_data <- lcms_long |>
  group_by(Compound, Stage) |>
  summarise(mean_abundance = mean(abundance, na.rm = TRUE), .groups = "drop") |>
  group_by(Compound) |>
  mutate(z = as.numeric(scale(mean_abundance))) |>
  ungroup()

clust_matrix <- heatmap_data |>
  select(Compound, Stage, z) |>
  pivot_wider(names_from = Stage, values_from = z) |>
  column_to_rownames("Compound") |>
  as.matrix()

compound_order <- rownames(clust_matrix)[hclust(dist(clust_matrix))$order]

heatmap_data <- heatmap_data |>
  mutate(Compound = factor(Compound, levels = compound_order))

ggplot(heatmap_data, aes(x = Stage, y = Compound, fill = z)) +
  geom_tile() +
  scale_fill_gradient2(low = "steelblue", mid = "white", high = "firebrick", midpoint = 0) +
  labs(title = "Metabolite abundance by Stage (row z-scored)",
       x = "Stage", y = NULL, fill = "z-score") +
  theme(axis.text.y = element_text(size = 12)) 
```

## One-way ANOVA per compound across Diagnosis/Stage groups

`Stage` has 5 levels: `-` (Control, n = 76) and cancer Stages 1-4
(n = 19, 49, 47, 20). For each of the 99 compounds we fit a one-way ANOVA of
log2-transformed abundance on `Stage`, then correct the 99 resulting p-values
for multiple testing with the Benjamini-Hochberg (FDR) method.

Abundances include exact zeros, so a small pseudocount (half the smallest
observed non-zero abundance) is added before log-transforming.

```{r}
library(broom)

min_pos <- min(lcms_long$abundance[lcms_long$abundance > 0], na.rm = TRUE)

lcms_long_log <- lcms_long |>
  mutate(log_abundance = log2(abundance + min_pos / 2))

anova_results <- lcms_long_log |>
  group_by(Compound) |>
  nest() |>
  mutate(
    model = map(data, ~ aov(log_abundance ~ Stage, data = .x)),
    tidy_model = map(model, broom::tidy)
  ) |>
  select(Compound, tidy_model) |>
  unnest(tidy_model) |>
  filter(term == "Stage") |>
  ungroup() |>
  mutate(p_adj_BH = p.adjust(p.value, method = "BH")) |>
  arrange(p_adj_BH)

anova_results |> select(Compound, df, statistic, p.value, p_adj_BH)
sum(anova_results$p_adj_BH < 0.05)
```

### Why log-transform? Skewness before and after

Raw abundances are right-skewed for most compounds, which motivates the
log2-transformation used above. We quantify skewness per compound on the
raw scale and on the log2 scale to confirm the transform actually reduces
it.

```{r}
skewness_fn <- function(x) {
  x <- x[!is.na(x)]
  n <- length(x)
  (sum((x - mean(x))^3) / n) / sd(x)^3
}

skew_compare <- lcms_long_log |>
  group_by(Compound) |>
  summarise(
    skewness_raw = skewness_fn(abundance),
    skewness_log = skewness_fn(log_abundance),
    .groups = "drop"
  )

summary(skew_compare$skewness_raw)
summary(skew_compare$skewness_log)

# How many compounds are "highly skewed" (|skewness| > 1) on each scale
sum(abs(skew_compare$skewness_raw) > 1, na.rm = TRUE)
sum(abs(skew_compare$skewness_log) > 1, na.rm = TRUE)
```

```{r, fig.width=9, fig.height=4}
skew_compare_long <- skew_compare |>
  pivot_longer(starts_with("skewness"), names_to = "scale", values_to = "skewness") |>
  mutate(scale = recode(scale, skewness_raw = "Raw abundance", skewness_log = "Log2 abundance"),
         scale = factor(scale, levels = c("Raw abundance", "Log2 abundance")))

ggplot(skew_compare_long, aes(x = skewness)) +
  geom_histogram(binwidth = 0.5, boundary = 0) +
  geom_vline(xintercept = 0, linetype = "dashed") +
  facet_wrap(~scale, scales = "free_y") +
  labs(title = "Per-compound skewness: raw vs. log2-transformed abundance",
       x = "Skewness", y = "# compounds (of 99)")
```

Raw abundances are overwhelmingly right-skewed: median skewness is 1.78,
and 74 of 99 compounds have |skewness| > 1, almost all in the positive
(right-skewed) direction. On the log2 scale, median skewness moves close to
zero (-0.06) and only 28 of 99 compounds remain highly skewed (a mix of
residual right- and left-skew). Log2-transforming substantially reduces
skewness overall -- supporting its use as the working scale for the ANOVA,
Tukey, and correlation analyses above -- though it does not fully normalize
every compound, consistent with the non-normal residuals noted in the
assumption checks below.

### Checking ANOVA assumptions

```{r}
library(car)

anova_diag <- lcms_long_log |>
  group_by(Compound) |>
  nest() |>
  mutate(
    model = map(data, ~ aov(log_abundance ~ Stage, data = .x)),
    shapiro_p = map_dbl(model, ~ shapiro.test(residuals(.x))$p.value),
    levene_p = map_dbl(data, ~ tryCatch(
      leveneTest(log_abundance ~ Stage, data = .x)[1, "Pr(>F)"],
      error = function(e) NA_real_
    ))
  ) |>
  select(Compound, shapiro_p, levene_p) |>
  ungroup()

# Residuals are non-normal for many compounds even after log transform;
# a meaningful fraction also show unequal variance across groups.
cat("Non-normal residuals (Shapiro p < .05):", sum(anova_diag$shapiro_p < 0.05), "/", nrow(anova_diag), "\n")
cat("Unequal variances (Levene p < .05):    ", sum(anova_diag$levene_p < 0.05, na.rm = TRUE), "/", sum(!is.na(anova_diag$levene_p)), "\n")
```

Given the unequal variances flagged above (driven partly by the unbalanced group sizes), we cross-check with Welch's ANOVA, which does not assume equal variances.

```{r}
welch_results <- lcms_long_log |>
  group_by(Compound) |>
  nest() |>
  mutate(
    welch = map(data, ~ oneway.test(log_abundance ~ Stage, data = .x, var.equal = FALSE)),
    statistic = map_dbl(welch, "statistic"),
    p.value = map_dbl(welch, "p.value")
  ) |>
  select(Compound, statistic, p.value) |>
  ungroup() |>
  mutate(p_adj_BH = p.adjust(p.value, method = "BH")) |>
  arrange(p_adj_BH)

# Agreement between standard-ANOVA and Welch-ANOVA significance calls
# (rows = standard ANOVA sig., columns = Welch ANOVA sig.)
compare_sig <- anova_results |>
  select(Compound, p_adj_BH_std = p_adj_BH) |>
  left_join(welch_results |> select(Compound, p_adj_BH_welch = p_adj_BH), by = "Compound") |>
  mutate(sig_std = p_adj_BH_std < 0.05, sig_welch = p_adj_BH_welch < 0.05)

table(standard = compare_sig$sig_std, welch = compare_sig$sig_welch)
```

The two approaches agree on the vast majority of compounds, so the ANOVA
conclusions are not driven by the variance-homogeneity violation.

### Significant compounds (BH-adjusted p < 0.05)

```{r, fig.height=8}
sig_compounds <- anova_results |>
  filter(p_adj_BH < 0.05)

nrow(sig_compounds)

ggplot(sig_compounds, aes(x = -log10(p_adj_BH), y = reorder(Compound, -log10(p_adj_BH)))) +
  geom_col() +
  labs(title = "Compounds significant by Stage (one-way ANOVA, BH-adjusted)",
       x = expression(-log[10]~ "(adjusted p-value)"), y = NULL) +
  theme(axis.text.y = element_text(size = 10))
```

## Tukey HSD post-hoc tests on ANOVA-significant compounds

The omnibus ANOVA only tells us a compound differs *somewhere* across the 5 groups. For the 42 compounds significant at BH-adjusted p < 0.05, Tukey HSD identifies *which* pairs of groups (Control, Stage 1-4) differ, with the family-wise error rate controlled within each compound's set of 10 pairwise comparisons.

```{r}
sig_compound_names <- anova_results |> filter(p_adj_BH < 0.05) |> pull(Compound)

tukey_results <- lcms_long_log |>
  filter(Compound %in% sig_compound_names) |>
  group_by(Compound) |>
  nest() |>
  mutate(
    model = map(data, ~ aov(log_abundance ~ Stage, data = .x)),
    tukey = map(model, ~ broom::tidy(TukeyHSD(.x)))
  ) |>
  select(Compound, tukey) |>
  unnest(tukey) |>
  ungroup() |>
  select(Compound, contrast, estimate, adj.p.value)

tukey_results
```

### Which group pairs drive the differences?

```{r}
# Contrasts ending "--" involve Control (Stage level "-");
# all others compare two cancer stages.
contrast_summary <- tukey_results |>
  group_by(contrast) |>
  summarise(n_sig = sum(adj.p.value < 0.05), n_total = n(), .groups = "drop") |>
  mutate(contrast_type = ifelse(grepl("--$", contrast), "vs Control", "Stage vs Stage")) |>
  arrange(desc(n_sig))

contrast_summary |> print()

ggplot(contrast_summary, aes(x = n_sig, y = reorder(contrast, n_sig), fill = contrast_type)) +
  geom_col() +
  labs(title = "Significant Tukey pairs out of 42 ANOVA-significant compounds",
       x = "Number of compounds significant (adj. p < .05)", y = "Contrast", fill = NULL)
```

Differences are concentrated in the **Control vs. cancer** comparisons
(18-25 of 42 compounds significant for each Stage-vs-Control pair), while
**Stage-vs-Stage** comparisons among cancer cases are rarely significant
(0-5 of 42). This suggests the ANOVA signal detected above is driven mainly by cancer-vs-healthy differences rather than progression across cancer stages.

### Compounds with a significant Stage-vs-Stage difference

```{r}
tukey_results |>
  filter(!grepl("--$", contrast), adj.p.value < 0.05) |>
  arrange(adj.p.value) |> arrange(contrast) |> 
  print()
```

## Clustered correlation analysis of compounds

Using `lcms_long_log` (log2 abundance for all 99 compounds x 211 samples),
we compute pairwise **Spearman** correlations between compounds (Spearman
rather than Pearson given the non-normality documented above) and cluster
compounds by correlation structure (distance = 1 - correlation, average
linkage).

```{r}
library(tidyr)
library(tibble)

log_wide <- lcms_long_log |>
  select(Compound, sample_id, log_abundance) |>
  pivot_wider(names_from = sample_id, values_from = log_abundance) |>
  column_to_rownames("Compound") |>
  as.matrix()

cor_mat <- cor(t(log_wide), method = "spearman", use = "pairwise.complete.obs")
cor_dist <- as.dist(1 - cor_mat)
hc <- hclust(cor_dist, method = "average")
```

### Choosing the number of clusters

Average silhouette width is used to check whether the data support distinct
compound clusters, rather than picking a cluster count arbitrarily.

```{r}
library(cluster)

sil_widths <- sapply(2:15, function(k) {
  cl <- cutree(hc, k = k)
  mean(silhouette(cl, cor_dist)[, "sil_width"])
})

data.frame(k = 2:15, avg_sil_width = round(sil_widths, 3))
```

Silhouette widths stay low (< 0.2) across all tested k, indicating the
correlation structure among compounds is weak and diffuse rather than
organized into a small number of tight, well-separated modules. We display
k = 8 below for visualization, but the cluster boundaries should be read as
descriptive groupings, not as strongly-supported distinct biological
modules.

```{r, fig.height=11, fig.width=9}
library(pheatmap)

k_clusters <- 8
cluster_assignments <- cutree(hc, k = k_clusters)
annotation_row <- data.frame(cluster = factor(cluster_assignments))
rownames(annotation_row) <- names(cluster_assignments)

pheatmap(
  cor_mat,
  clustering_distance_rows = cor_dist,
  clustering_distance_cols = cor_dist,
  clustering_method = "average",
  annotation_row = annotation_row,
  show_colnames = FALSE,
  fontsize_row = 5,
  main = "Spearman correlation among compounds (clustered)",
  color = colorRampPalette(c("steelblue", "white", "firebrick"))(100),
  breaks = seq(-1, 1, length.out = 101)
)
```

Most off-diagonal correlations are weak (near white), consistent with the
low silhouette widths; a couple of tighter, more strongly-correlated
sub-blocks are visible nested within the larger clusters, which may be worth
inspecting individually (e.g. by compound class such as acylcarnitines).

## Sample-sample correlation, annotated by Stage

The compound-compound clustering above asks whether *compounds* group
together. Here we instead ask whether *samples* cluster by Stage: do
patients with the same Stage (or Control) have more similar overall
metabolite profiles than patients in different Stages?

```{r, fig.height=9, fig.width=9}
library(tibble)

sample_cor <- cor(log_wide, method = "spearman", use = "pairwise.complete.obs")
sample_dist <- as.dist(1 - sample_cor)
hc_samples <- hclust(sample_dist, method = "average")

stage_annotation <- metadata_merged |>
  select(sample_id, Stage) |>
  distinct() |>
  column_to_rownames("sample_id")
stage_annotation <- stage_annotation[colnames(sample_cor), , drop = FALSE]

stage_colors <- list(Stage = c(
  "-" = "grey70", "1" = "#fee8c8", "2" = "#fdbb84", "3" = "#e34a33", "4" = "#7f0000"
))

pheatmap(
  sample_cor,
  clustering_distance_rows = sample_dist,
  clustering_distance_cols = sample_dist,
  clustering_method = "average",
  annotation_row = stage_annotation,
  annotation_col = stage_annotation,
  annotation_colors = stage_colors,
  show_rownames = FALSE,
  show_colnames = FALSE,
  main = "Sample-sample Spearman correlation (annotated by Stage)",
  color = colorRampPalette(c("steelblue", "white", "firebrick"))(100),
  breaks = seq(min(sample_cor), 1, length.out = 101)
)
```

Visually the Stage color bar does not resolve into distinct blocks along the
dendrogram, suggesting Stage is not a dominant driver of overall sample
similarity. We quantify this directly by comparing mean pairwise correlation
for same-Stage vs. different-Stage sample pairs.

```{r}
cor_long <- as.data.frame(sample_cor) |>
  rownames_to_column("sample_a") |>
  pivot_longer(-sample_a, names_to = "sample_b", values_to = "r") |>
  filter(sample_a != sample_b) |>
  left_join(stage_annotation |> rownames_to_column("sample_a") |> rename(stage_a = Stage), by = "sample_a") |>
  left_join(stage_annotation |> rownames_to_column("sample_b") |> rename(stage_b = Stage), by = "sample_b") |>
  mutate(pair_type = ifelse(stage_a == stage_b, "same stage", "different stage"))

cor_long |>
  group_by(pair_type) |>
  summarise(mean_r = mean(r), median_r = median(r), n_pairs = n(), .groups = "drop")
```

Mean same-Stage correlation (~0.795) is only marginally higher than mean
different-Stage correlation (~0.789) — a difference of about 0.006, which is
not practically meaningful given correlations in the 0.47-1.0 range overall.
**Samples do not cluster by Stage** in their overall metabolite profile; the
Stage-associated signal detected by the ANOVA/Tukey analysis above is
confined to a subset of individual compounds rather than reflecting a
broad, sample-level Stage signature.

### Repeating on just the 42 ANOVA-significant compounds

Since the signal detected earlier lives in a subset of compounds, restricting
the sample-sample correlation to just those 42 compounds should make any
Control-vs-cancer signal more visible than it was across all 99 compounds.

```{r, fig.height=9, fig.width=9}
log_wide_sig <- log_wide[rownames(log_wide) %in% sig_compound_names, ]

sample_cor_sig <- cor(log_wide_sig, method = "spearman", use = "pairwise.complete.obs")
sample_dist_sig <- as.dist(1 - sample_cor_sig)
stage_annotation_sig <- stage_annotation[colnames(sample_cor_sig), , drop = FALSE]

pheatmap(
  sample_cor_sig,
  clustering_distance_rows = sample_dist_sig,
  clustering_distance_cols = sample_dist_sig,
  clustering_method = "average",
  annotation_row = stage_annotation_sig,
  annotation_col = stage_annotation_sig,
  annotation_colors = stage_colors,
  show_rownames = FALSE,
  show_colnames = FALSE,
  main = "Sample-sample Spearman correlation, 42 ANOVA-significant compounds only",
  color = colorRampPalette(c("steelblue", "white", "firebrick"))(100),
  breaks = seq(min(sample_cor_sig), 1, length.out = 101)
)
```

```{r}
cor_long_sig <- as.data.frame(sample_cor_sig) |>
  rownames_to_column("sample_a") |>
  pivot_longer(-sample_a, names_to = "sample_b", values_to = "r") |>
  filter(sample_a != sample_b) |>
  left_join(stage_annotation_sig |> rownames_to_column("sample_a") |> rename(stage_a = Stage), by = "sample_a") |>
  left_join(stage_annotation_sig |> rownames_to_column("sample_b") |> rename(stage_b = Stage), by = "sample_b") |>
  mutate(pair_type = ifelse(stage_a == stage_b, "same stage", "different stage"))

cor_long_sig |>
  group_by(pair_type) |>
  summarise(mean_r = mean(r), median_r = median(r), n_pairs = n(), .groups = "drop")

# Collapse to Control vs Cancer to test the specific signal found by ANOVA/Tukey
cor_long_sig |>
  mutate(
    group_a = ifelse(stage_a == "-", "Control", "Cancer"),
    group_b = ifelse(stage_b == "-", "Control", "Cancer"),
    diag_pair_type = paste(pmin(group_a, group_b), pmax(group_a, group_b), sep = " - ")
  ) |>
  group_by(diag_pair_type) |>
  summarise(mean_r = mean(r), median_r = median(r), n_pairs = n(), .groups = "drop")
```

Restricting to the 42 significant compounds sharpens the pattern somewhat:
same-Stage mean correlation (0.784) exceeds different-Stage (0.768) by about
0.016 — small but roughly 3x the gap seen across all 99 compounds. More
informative is the Control/Cancer split: **Cancer-Cancer** sample pairs
correlate most strongly (mean r = 0.808), clearly above **Cancer-Control**
(0.743) and **Control-Control** (0.757) pairs. This matches the Tukey
result — cancer samples share a more consistent profile across these 42
compounds than either controls do among themselves or cancer/control pairs
do with each other — but the effect is a shift in central tendency, not a
clean visual separation into blocks in the heatmap above, and cancer Stages
1-4 remain thoroughly intermixed with each other.



## Mean sample-sampel correlations by stage pair (42 sig metabolites)

```{r}
stage_matrix_full <- cor_long |>
  group_by(stage_a, stage_b) |>
  summarise(mean_r = mean(r), .groups = "drop") |>
  pivot_wider(names_from = stage_b, values_from = mean_r)

stage_matrix_sig <- cor_long_sig |>
  group_by(stage_a, stage_b) |>
  summarise(mean_r = mean(r), .groups = "drop") |>
  pivot_wider(names_from = stage_b, values_from = mean_r)

cat("All 99 compounds:\n")
print(stage_matrix_full)
```

```{r}
cat("\n42 ANOVA-significant compounds:\n")

print(stage_matrix_sig)
```

```{r}
stage_matrix_sig_long <- cor_long_sig |>
  group_by(stage_a, stage_b) |>
  summarise(mean_r = mean(r), .groups = "drop")

ggplot(stage_matrix_sig_long, aes(x = stage_a, y = stage_b, fill = mean_r)) +
  geom_tile() +
  geom_text(aes(label = round(mean_r, 3)), size = 3.5) +
  scale_fill_gradient2(low = "steelblue", mid = "white", high = "firebrick", midpoint = 0.78) +
  labs(title = "Mean sample-sample correlation by Stage pair (42 sig. compounds)",
       x = "Stage", y = "Stage", fill = "mean r")
```

## PCA scores: does PC1 vs PC2 separate by Stage?

The correlation analyses above show Control separates from Cancer, but
individual cancer Stages do not separate from each other. We check whether
a PCA scores plot shows the same pattern -- both across all 86 complete-case
compounds, and restricted to the 42 ANOVA-significant compounds (where the
Stage/Diagnosis signal is concentrated).

`log_wide` (built above for the compound-compound correlation analysis) still
has 13 compounds with at least one missing value; `prcomp()` requires
complete data, so we restrict to the 86 compounds with no missing values
rather than imputing here.

```{r}
complete_compounds <- lcms_long_log |>
  group_by(Compound) |>
  summarise(any_na = any(is.na(log_abundance)), .groups = "drop") |>
  filter(!any_na) |>
  pull(Compound)

length(complete_compounds)

log_wide_complete <- log_wide[rownames(log_wide) %in% complete_compounds, ]

pca_fit <- prcomp(t(log_wide_complete), scale. = TRUE)

pca_scores <- as.data.frame(pca_fit$x[, 1:2]) |>
  rownames_to_column("sample_id") |>
  left_join(metadata_merged |> select(sample_id, Diagnosis, Stage) |> distinct(), by = "sample_id")
```

```{r}
var_pc1 <- round(summary(pca_fit)$importance[2, "PC1"] * 100, 1)
var_pc2 <- round(summary(pca_fit)$importance[2, "PC2"] * 100, 1)

stage_colors_vec <- c("-" = "grey60", "1" = "#fee8c8", "2" = "#fdbb84", "3" = "#e34a33", "4" = "#7f0000")

ggplot(pca_scores, aes(x = PC1, y = PC2, color = Stage)) +
  geom_point(alpha = 0.7) +
  scale_color_manual(values = stage_colors_vec) +
  labs(title = "PCA (86 compounds, complete cases)",
       x = paste0("PC1 (", var_pc1, "%)"), y = paste0("PC2 (", var_pc2, "%)"))
```

Using all 86 complete-case compounds, PC1/PC2 (together explaining only
~24.9% of variance) show no visible separation by Stage or Control -- points
of every Stage are thoroughly intermixed. This makes sense: most of these
86 compounds are not associated with Diagnosis/Stage, so their variance
dilutes any real signal.

### Restricting to the 42 ANOVA-significant compounds

Missing values in 5 of the 42 compounds (57 values total, mostly
Pentosidine) are imputed with the per-compound median for this PCA, since
`prcomp()` requires complete data.

```{r, fig.width=10, fig.height=5}
library(tibble)
library(patchwork)

log_wide_sig_imputed <- t(apply(log_wide_sig, 1, function(x) {
  x[is.na(x)] <- median(x, na.rm = TRUE)
  x
}))

pca_fit_sig <- prcomp(t(log_wide_sig_imputed), scale. = TRUE)
var_pc1_sig <- round(summary(pca_fit_sig)$importance[2, "PC1"] * 100, 1)
var_pc2_sig <- round(summary(pca_fit_sig)$importance[2, "PC2"] * 100, 1)

pca_scores_sig <- as.data.frame(pca_fit_sig$x[, 1:2]) |>
  rownames_to_column("sample_id") |>
  left_join(metadata_merged |> select(sample_id, Diagnosis, Stage) |> distinct(), by = "sample_id")

p_pca_sig_stage <- ggplot(pca_scores_sig, aes(x = PC1, y = PC2, color = Stage)) +
  geom_point(alpha = 0.7) +
  scale_color_manual(values = stage_colors_vec) +
  labs(title = "By Stage", x = paste0("PC1 (", var_pc1_sig, "%)"), y = paste0("PC2 (", var_pc2_sig, "%)")) + theme_bw()

p_pca_sig_diag <- ggplot(pca_scores_sig, aes(x = PC1, y = PC2, color = Diagnosis)) +
  geom_point(alpha = 0.7) +
  labs(title = "By Diagnosis", x = paste0("PC1 (", var_pc1_sig, "%)"), y = paste0("PC2 (", var_pc2_sig, "%)")) +
  theme_bw()

p_pca_sig_stage | p_pca_sig_diag
```

```{r}
pca_scores_sig |>
  group_by(Diagnosis) |>
  summarise(mean_PC1 = mean(PC1), mean_PC2 = mean(PC2), n = n())

pca_scores_sig |>
  filter(Diagnosis == "Breast cancer") |>
  group_by(Stage) |>
  summarise(mean_PC1 = mean(PC1), mean_PC2 = mean(PC2), n = n())
```

Restricted to the 42 significant compounds, a pattern emerges: Control
samples occupy mostly positive PC2 (mean PC2 = 1.51) while cancer samples
skew negative (mean PC2 = -0.85) -- visible as Control (grey/teal) points
concentrating in the upper region of the plot. This is consistent with the
Control-vs-cancer signal detected by ANOVA/Tukey and the sample-correlation
analysis. However, among cancer cases, Stages 1-4 do **not** separate from
each other -- their mean PC1/PC2 values overlap substantially (e.g. Stage 3
mean PC2 = -1.19 vs. Stage 4 mean PC2 = -1.10) and points of all four
Stages are intermixed within the "cancer" region. This matches every prior
analysis: the detectable signal in this dataset is Control vs. Cancer, not
Stage progression.


### Which compounds drive the PC2 (Control-vs-Cancer) separation?

Since Control-vs-Cancer separates along **PC2** (not PC1) in the
42-compound PCA, we rank compounds by the magnitude of their PC2 loading.

```{r}
loadings_sig <- as.data.frame(pca_fit_sig$rotation[, 1:2]) |>
  rownames_to_column("Compound") |>
  rename(loading_PC1 = PC1, loading_PC2 = PC2) |>
  arrange(desc(abs(loading_PC2)))

loadings_sig |> select(Compound, loading_PC1, loading_PC2) |> head(15)
```

To confirm these loadings correspond to a real Control-vs-Cancer
difference (and not just an artifact of the rotation), we compare each
top compound's actual mean log2-abundance by Diagnosis.

```{r}
top_pc2_compounds <- loadings_sig |> slice_head(n = 15) |> pull(Compound)

lcms_long_log |>
  filter(Compound %in% top_pc2_compounds) |>
  group_by(Compound, Diagnosis) |>
  summarise(mean_log_abundance = mean(log_abundance, na.rm = TRUE), .groups = "drop") |>
  pivot_wider(names_from = Diagnosis, values_from = mean_log_abundance) |>
  mutate(higher_in = ifelse(`Breast cancer` > Control, "Cancer", "Control")) |>
  left_join(loadings_sig |> select(Compound, loading_PC2), by = "Compound") |>
  arrange(desc(abs(loading_PC2))) |> 
  print()
```

The top PC2 loadings are dominated by **Phenyllactic acid** and
**Pentosidine** (both higher in Control) and **Glutamine**, **Lysine**,
and **Sphingosine 1-phosphate** (all higher in Cancer), along with several
medium-chain acylcarnitines (Dodecanoyl-, Octanoyl-, Hexanoyl-,
Decanoylcarnitine). Loading sign broadly tracks actual Control-vs-Cancer
direction for most of these compounds, but not perfectly (e.g.
Dodecanoylcarnitine's positive loading doesn't match its higher-in-Cancer
direction) -- expected in a multivariate rotation where a compound's PC2
contribution reflects its correlation with *all* other compounds jointly,
not just its own univariate Control-vs-Cancer difference. For a purely
univariate ranking of Control-vs-Cancer effects, the ANOVA/Tukey results
earlier in this document are the more direct reference.




### Plotting compounds driving PC2 separation

```{r, fig.height=10}
#library(forcats)

plot_data <- lcms_long_log |>
  filter(Compound %in% top_pc2_compounds) |>
  mutate(Compound = fct_relevel(Compound, top_pc2_compounds))

ggplot(plot_data, aes(x = Diagnosis, y = log_abundance, fill = Diagnosis)) +
  geom_boxplot(outlier.size = 0.8) +
  facet_wrap(~Compound, scales = "free_y", ncol = 5) +
  labs(title = "Top 15 compounds driving PC2 (Control vs Cancer separation)",
       x = "Diagnosis", y = "log2(abundance)") +
  theme_gray(base_size = 18) +
  theme(legend.position = "top")
  
```

### Significance is added via a Wilcoxon rank-sum test (Control vs. Cancer,
appropriate given the non-normality documented earlier) per compound,
BH-corrected across these 15 tests.

```{r, fig.width=11, fig.height=8}
library(rstatix)
library(ggpubr)

plot_data <- lcms_long_log |>
  filter(Compound %in% top_pc2_compounds) |>
  mutate(Compound = fct_relevel(Compound, top_pc2_compounds))

stat_test <- plot_data |>
  group_by(Compound) |>
  wilcox_test(log_abundance ~ Diagnosis) |>
  adjust_pvalue(method = "BH") |>
  add_significance("p.adj") |>
  add_xy_position(x = "Diagnosis", fun = "max", step.increase = 0.08)

stat_test |> select(Compound, group1, group2, p, p.adj, p.adj.signif)

ggplot(plot_data, aes(x = Diagnosis, y = log_abundance, fill = Diagnosis)) +
  geom_boxplot(outlier.size = 0.8) +
  stat_pvalue_manual(stat_test, label = "p.adj.signif", tip.length = 0.01, hide.ns = FALSE) +
  facet_wrap(~Compound, scales = "free_y", ncol = 5) +
  labs(title = "Top 15 compounds driving PC2 (Control vs Cancer separation)",
       subtitle = "Wilcoxon rank-sum test, BH-adjusted: * p<.05, ** p<.01, *** p<.001, **** p<.0001",
       x = NULL, y = "log2(abundance)") +
  theme(legend.position = "top", strip.text = element_text(size = 7))
```

The boxplots confirm the direction-check table visually: Phenyllactic acid,
Pentosidine, Glycerophosphocholine, and Progesterone are visibly higher in
Control, while Glutamine, Lysine, and Sphingosine 1-phosphate are visibly
higher in Cancer. All 15 remain significant after BH correction, but effect
clarity varies -- the acylcarnitines (Dodecanoyl-, Octanoyl-, Hexanoyl-,
Decanoylcarnitine) show the weakest significance (`*`, adj. p roughly
0.01-0.04) and the most visually overlapping distributions, consistent with
their weaker, less consistent contribution to PC2 noted above.

## Mapping significant metabolites onto KEGG pathways

The 42 ANOVA-significant compounds all have a significant Control-vs-Stage
Tukey pair (i.e. the Control-vs-cancer-driven set identified earlier is
identical to the full ANOVA-significant set). We map these 42 compound
names onto KEGG compound IDs, then onto KEGG pathways, using `KEGGREST`.
(`MetaboAnalystR` was considered for this step but skipped -- it requires a
heavy, GitHub-only install with many Bioconductor dependencies, whereas
KEGGREST's `compound`/`pathway` REST endpoints cover what we need directly.)

Name resolution is not fully automatic: many compound names in this
dataset don't exactly match KEGG's canonical synonyms (e.g. KEGG stores
"Butyrylcarnitine" as "O-Butanoylcarnitine", "Homocysteic acid" as
"L-Homocysteic acid"). We first try an exact case-insensitive match against
KEGG's synonym list (stripping common prefixes like `O-`/`L-`/`D-`/`N6-`),
then manually verify a handful of remaining names against candidate KEGG
entries.

```{r}
library(KEGGREST)

control_vs_cancer_sig <- tukey_results |>
  filter(grepl("--$", contrast), adj.p.value < 0.05) |>
  distinct(Compound) |>
  pull(Compound)

length(control_vs_cancer_sig)  # identical to the 42 ANOVA-significant compounds

strip_prefixes <- function(x) {
  x <- tolower(x)
  x <- gsub("^(o-|l-|d-|n6-|n-|\\(r\\)-|\\(s\\)-)", "", x)
  trimws(x)
}

resolve_kegg <- function(name) {
  hits <- tryCatch(keggFind("compound", name), error = function(e) NULL)
  if (is.null(hits) || length(hits) == 0) return(NA_character_)
  target <- strip_prefixes(name)
  for (i in seq_along(hits)) {
    syns <- str_split(hits[i], ";")[[1]] |> str_trim() |> strip_prefixes()
    if (any(syns == target)) return(names(hits)[i])
  }
  # fall back to unstripped exact match
  for (i in seq_along(hits)) {
    syns <- str_split(hits[i], ";")[[1]] |> str_trim()
    if (any(tolower(syns) == tolower(name))) return(names(hits)[i])
  }
  NA_character_
}

kegg_map <- tibble(Compound = control_vs_cancer_sig) |>
  mutate(kegg_id_raw = map_chr(Compound, resolve_kegg))

# A handful of names needed manual verification against candidate KEGG
# entries (e.g. confirming "Phenyllactic acid" -> C05607 "Phenyllactate",
# not the superficially similar but biologically distinct C01207
# "3-(3,4-Dihydroxyphenyl)lactate" that a naive fuzzy match would suggest).
manual_matches <- c(
  "Octanoylcarnitine" = "C02838",
  "Butyrylcarnitine" = "C02862",
  "Propionylcarnitine" = "C03017",
  "Decanoylcarnitine" = "C03299",
  "Homocysteic acid" = "C16511",
  "Phenyllactic acid" = "C05607",
  "6-Phosphogluconic acid" = "C00345",
  "Delta-hydroxylysine" = "C16741"
)

kegg_map_final <- kegg_map |>
  mutate(kegg_id = ifelse(is.na(kegg_id_raw), manual_matches[Compound], kegg_id_raw)) |>
  select(Compound, kegg_id)

kegg_map_final |> count(matched = !is.na(kegg_id))
kegg_map_final |> filter(is.na(kegg_id))
```

29 of 42 compounds (69%) resolve to a KEGG compound ID. The 13 that don't
were checked against multiple synonym variants each and genuinely have no
entry in KEGG's compound database -- mostly longer-chain acylcarnitines
(Dodecanoyl-, Hexanoyl-, Stearoyl-, Tetradecanoylcarnitine, Linoleyl
carnitine, oleoylcarnitine, trans-Hexadec-2-enoyl carnitine), the free form
of Pentosidine (only a protein-bound form, `[Protein]-pentosidine`, exists
in KEGG), and a few others (3-Indolepropionic acid, 3-Pyridylacetic acid,
Bisnorcholic acid, Succinyladenosine, 4,8-dimethylnonanoyl carnitine). This
is a genuine coverage gap in KEGG (it curates core metabolic pathway
compounds rather than the full space of lipid/exotic metabolite species),
not a search failure.

### Which pathways do the mapped compounds belong to?

Generic KEGG overview/global maps (e.g. "Metabolic pathways",
"Biosynthesis of secondary metabolites") are excluded, since they aren't
specific enough to be informative.

```{r}
EXCLUDE <- c(
  "map01100", "map01110", "map01120", "map01200", "map01210", "map01230",
  "map01240", "map01250", "map01220", "map01310", "map01320",
  "map01060", "map01061", "map01062", "map01063", "map01064", "map01065",
  "map01066", "map01070", "map00996", "map00997", "map00998", "map00999",
  "map00975", "map02010", "map02020"
)

mapped_ids <- kegg_map_final |> filter(!is.na(kegg_id)) |> pull(kegg_id)
pathway_links <- keggLink("pathway", mapped_ids)

path_names_raw <- keggList("pathway", "hsa")
path_names <- tibble(
  path = paste0("map", substr(names(path_names_raw), 4, 8)),
  pathway_name = sub(" - Homo sapiens.*", "", path_names_raw)
) |> distinct(path, .keep_all = TRUE)

pathway_df <- tibble(
  cpd = sub("^cpd:", "", names(pathway_links)),
  path = sub("^path:", "", pathway_links)
) |>
  filter(!path %in% EXCLUDE) |>
  left_join(kegg_map_final |> rename(cpd = kegg_id), by = "cpd") |>
  left_join(path_names, by = "path") |>
  mutate(pathway_name = ifelse(is.na(pathway_name), path, pathway_name))

pathway_summary <- pathway_df |>
  group_by(path, pathway_name) |>
  summarise(
    n_compounds = n_distinct(Compound),
    compounds = paste(sort(unique(Compound)), collapse = ", "),
    .groups = "drop"
  ) |>
  arrange(desc(n_compounds))

pathway_summary |> select(pathway_name, n_compounds, compounds)
```

```{r, fig.height=6}
plot_df <- pathway_summary |> filter(n_compounds >= 2) |> arrange(n_compounds)

ggplot(plot_df, aes(x = n_compounds, y = reorder(pathway_name, n_compounds))) +
  geom_col() +
  labs(title = "KEGG pathways containing >=2 of the 29 mapped, significant compounds",
       x = "Number of compounds", y = NULL)
```

The mapped compounds are spread thinly across many pathways -- most
pathways contain only 1-2 of our compounds, reflecting that these 29
metabolites span diverse core metabolic processes (amino acid, lipid,
nucleotide, and steroid metabolism) rather than concentrating in one
pathway. A few pathways of note given breast-cancer relevance: **Choline
metabolism in cancer**, **Pathways in cancer**, and **Prostate cancer**
each contain 2 compounds, and **Steroid hormone biosynthesis** /
**Ovarian steroidogenesis** (Androstenedione, Progesterone) reflect the
hormone-related compounds in the panel. This mapping is descriptive; it
does not yet test whether any pathway is significantly *over-represented*
relative to chance (that would require a formal enrichment test, e.g. a
hypergeometric test against a defined background, as a natural next step).

### Formal hypergeometric enrichment test

As discussed earlier, the background ("population") for this test is the
**99 compounds actually measured on this platform** -- not the full KEGG
compound database -- since testing against the full KEGG universe would
overstate significance for pathways that happen to overlap with what this
assay can detect. We map all 99 compounds to KEGG IDs (reusing the
manually-verified IDs from the 42 significant compounds above; the
remaining ~57 non-significant compounds use automated matching only, since
they don't need the same scrutiny as the compounds driving our
conclusions).

```{r}
all_99_compounds <- unique(lcms_long$Compound)

kegg_map_all <- tibble(Compound = all_99_compounds) |>
  mutate(kegg_id_raw = map_chr(Compound, resolve_kegg)) |>
  mutate(kegg_id = ifelse(is.na(kegg_id_raw) & Compound %in% names(manual_matches),
                           manual_matches[Compound], kegg_id_raw)) |>
  select(Compound, kegg_id)

# Prefer the manually-verified IDs for the 42 significant compounds
kegg_map_universe <- kegg_map_all |>
  left_join(kegg_map_final |> rename(kegg_id_verified = kegg_id), by = "Compound") |>
  mutate(kegg_id = coalesce(kegg_id_verified, kegg_id)) |>
  select(Compound, kegg_id)

sum(!is.na(kegg_map_universe$kegg_id))  # of 99 total
```

61 of 99 measured compounds (62%) resolve to a KEGG ID -- a similar hit
rate to the 42-compound panel. We retrieve pathway links for this full
background set, then run a one-sided hypergeometric test per pathway:
given `n_population` background compounds with a pathway annotation,
`n_sample` of which are our significant compounds, and `K` background
compounds in a given pathway, what's the probability of seeing `k` or more
significant compounds in that pathway by chance?

```{r}
bg_ids <- kegg_map_universe |> filter(!is.na(kegg_id)) |> pull(kegg_id)
bg_pathway_links <- keggLink("pathway", bg_ids)

bg_pathway_df <- tibble(
  cpd = sub("^cpd:", "", names(bg_pathway_links)),
  path = sub("^path:", "", bg_pathway_links)
) |>
  filter(!path %in% EXCLUDE) |>
  left_join(kegg_map_universe |> rename(cpd = kegg_id), by = "cpd")

n_population <- bg_pathway_df |> distinct(Compound) |> nrow()
n_sample <- pathway_df |> distinct(Compound) |> nrow()

bg_counts <- bg_pathway_df |>
  group_by(path) |>
  summarise(K = n_distinct(Compound), .groups = "drop")

hit_counts <- pathway_df |>
  group_by(path, pathway_name) |>
  summarise(k = n_distinct(Compound),
            hit_compounds = paste(sort(unique(Compound)), collapse = ", "),
            .groups = "drop")

enrichment <- hit_counts |>
  left_join(bg_counts, by = "path") |>
  mutate(
    p_value = phyper(k - 1, K, n_population - K, n_sample, lower.tail = FALSE),
    p_adj = p.adjust(p_value, method = "BH")
  ) |>
  arrange(p_value)

n_sample      # significant, pathway-annotated compounds tested
n_population  # background, pathway-annotated compounds tested

enrichment |> select(pathway_name, k, K, p_value, p_adj, hit_compounds) |> head(10)
```

**No pathway reaches significance after BH correction** -- the best
nominal p-value (Neuroactive ligand-receptor interaction, 3/3 hit
compounds) is 0.084, which becomes 0.65 after adjusting for the 83
pathways tested. This null result should be taken at face value rather
than over-interpreted from the raw ranking: only 22 of the 42 significant
compounds have any non-generic KEGG pathway annotation, tested against a
49-compound background -- a very small sample for a hypergeometric test to
have meaningful power. This mirrors a common limitation in untargeted
metabolomics pathway analysis: incomplete database coverage of measured
compounds constrains not just compound identification but also downstream
enrichment power, and the platform-specific background (however more
statistically appropriate than the full KEGG universe) further reduces the
population size available for testing. The pathway *mapping* above remains
useful as a descriptive/hypothesis-generating summary; it should not be
read as demonstrating statistically-supported pathway-level dysregulation.

### Sensitivity check: full KEGG compound database as background

For contrast, we rerun the identical test but swap the background for the
**entire KEGG compound universe** (all compounds appearing in any
non-generic pathway map) instead of the 99 measured compounds. This is the
default in many enrichment tools, but it is the **less conservative,
less defensible** choice here: it implicitly assumes our assay could have
detected any KEGG compound, which is false for a targeted panel, and it
therefore tends to overstate significance.

```{r}
bg_all_raw <- keggLink("pathway", "compound")

bg_all <- tibble(
  cpd  = sub("^cpd:", "", names(bg_all_raw)),
  path = sub("^path:", "", bg_all_raw)
) |>
  filter(grepl("^map", path), !path %in% EXCLUDE)

n_population_full <- bg_all |> distinct(cpd) |> nrow()

bg_counts_full <- bg_all |>
  group_by(path) |>
  summarise(K = n_distinct(cpd), .groups = "drop")

enrichment_full <- hit_counts |>
  left_join(bg_counts_full, by = "path") |>
  mutate(
    p_value = phyper(k - 1, K, n_population_full - K, n_sample, lower.tail = FALSE),
    p_adj   = p.adjust(p_value, method = "BH")
  ) |>
  arrange(p_value)

n_population_full                          # full-KEGG background size
sum(enrichment_full$p_adj < 0.05)          # pathways significant after BH

enrichment_full |> select(pathway_name, k, K, p_value, p_adj, hit_compounds) |> head(15)
```

Against the full KEGG background (`r n_population_full` compounds), the
**conclusion flips: 11 pathways now pass BH correction at p_adj < 0.05**,
including Glyoxylate and dicarboxylate metabolism, Choline metabolism in
cancer, Prolactin signaling, Prostate cancer, D-amino acid metabolism,
Ovarian steroidogenesis, Alanine/aspartate/glutamate metabolism, and
Pathways in cancer. The *hit compounds* are identical to the descriptive
mapping -- what changed is only the denominator. With ~6,300 background
compounds instead of 49, finding 2-4 of our compounds concentrated in a
small pathway looks far more surprising by chance, so the p-values shrink
dramatically.

This side-by-side is the whole point of the background-choice discussion:
the *same data* yields "nothing significant" or "11 significant pathways"
depending entirely on the reference set. The platform-restricted background
(previous section) is the more honest choice for a targeted panel, so these
11 hits should be read as **suggestive, not confirmatory** -- the full-KEGG
result is best treated as an upper bound on what enrichment might look like
with a fully-annotated, untargeted platform.

## Predictive modeling: classifying Control vs. Cancer with PLS-DA

Every analysis above points to a Control-vs-Cancer signal (not stage). Here
we test how well that signal supports *classification* of an individual
sample as Control or Breast cancer, using PLS-DA (partial least squares
discriminant analysis) -- a standard supervised method for high-dimensional,
correlated metabolomics predictors.

**Avoiding feature-selection leakage.** The 42 "significant" compounds were
chosen using an ANOVA on the *full* dataset. If we simply fed those into a
classifier and evaluated on a held-out subset, the test set would have
already influenced feature selection, inflating apparent performance. To
avoid this, we split first, then re-run the ANOVA/BH selection **using only
the training set**, so the test set plays no role in choosing predictors.

### Train/test split and leakage-free feature selection

```{r}
library(tidymodels)
library(plsmod)
library(tibble)

# Wide design matrix: all 99 compounds (log2) x samples, outcome = Diagnosis
modeling_df <- lcms_long_log |>
  select(Compound, sample_id, log_abundance) |>
  pivot_wider(names_from = Compound, values_from = log_abundance) |>
  left_join(metadata_merged |> select(sample_id, Diagnosis) |> distinct(),
            by = "sample_id") |>
  mutate(Diagnosis = factor(Diagnosis, levels = c("Control", "Breast cancer"))) |>
  column_to_rownames("sample_id")

set.seed(4127)
split <- initial_split(modeling_df, strata = Diagnosis)
train <- training(split)
test  <- testing(split)

# Re-select significant compounds using TRAINING DATA ONLY
train_ids <- rownames(train)
anova_results_train <- lcms_long_log |>
  filter(sample_id %in% train_ids) |>
  group_by(Compound) |>
  nest() |>
  mutate(
    model = map(data, ~ aov(log_abundance ~ Stage, data = .x)),
    tidy_model = map(model, broom::tidy)
  ) |>
  select(Compound, tidy_model) |>
  unnest(tidy_model) |>
  filter(term == "Stage") |>
  ungroup() |>
  mutate(p_adj_BH = p.adjust(p.value, method = "BH"))

predictor_cols <- anova_results_train |> filter(p_adj_BH < 0.05) |> pull(Compound)
length(predictor_cols)  # training-only significant compounds

train_final <- train[, c(predictor_cols, "Diagnosis")]
test_final  <- test[, c(predictor_cols, "Diagnosis")]
```

Training-only selection yields 27 compounds (fewer than the 42 from the full
data, as expected with a smaller sample), all of which are a subset of the
original 42.

### Cross-validation setup and null baseline

```{r}
set.seed(6183)
folds <- vfold_cv(train_final, v = 10, strata = Diagnosis)

metrics_class <- metric_set(roc_auc, accuracy, brier_class)

# Null baseline: always predicts the majority class
null_wf <- workflow() |>
  add_recipe(recipe(Diagnosis ~ ., data = train_final) |>
               step_impute_median(all_numeric_predictors())) |>
  add_model(null_model(mode = "classification") |> set_engine("parsnip"))

null_res <- fit_resamples(null_wf, resamples = folds, metrics = metrics_class)
collect_metrics(null_res) |> select(.metric, mean, std_err)
```

The class split is 64% cancer / 36% control, so the null model reaches
0.64 accuracy but ROC AUC of exactly 0.50 -- it has no discriminative
ability, which is the bar PLS-DA must clear.

### PLS-DA: tuning the number of components

Missing values (Pentosidine, Phenyllactic acid) are median-imputed and
predictors normalized inside the recipe, so both are refit within each
resample fold. The only hyperparameter is the number of latent components.

```{r}
pls_wf <- workflow() |>
  add_recipe(
    recipe(Diagnosis ~ ., data = train_final) |>
      step_impute_median(all_numeric_predictors()) |>
      step_normalize(all_numeric_predictors())
  ) |>
  add_model(pls(num_comp = tune()) |> set_engine("mixOmics") |> set_mode("classification"))

set.seed(7321)
pls_tune <- tune_grid(
  pls_wf,
  resamples = folds,
  grid = tibble(num_comp = 1:10),
  metrics = metrics_class
)

collect_metrics(pls_tune) |>
  filter(.metric == "roc_auc") |>
  select(num_comp, mean, std_err) |>
  arrange(desc(mean))
```

ROC AUC peaks at `num_comp = 2` (CV mean 0.985) and is essentially flat for
2-6 components, so we take the most parsimonious choice, 2 components.

### Final model: held-out test-set evaluation

```{r}
pls_final_wf <- finalize_workflow(pls_wf, tibble(num_comp = 2))

cv_metrics <- collect_metrics(pls_tune) |>
  filter(num_comp == 2) |>
  select(.metric, cv_mean = mean, cv_std_err = std_err)

pls_fit <- fit(pls_final_wf, data = train_final)

test_pred <- test_final |>
  bind_cols(predict(pls_fit, test_final, type = "prob")) |>
  bind_cols(predict(pls_fit, test_final, type = "class"))

test_metrics <- bind_rows(
  roc_auc(test_pred, truth = Diagnosis, .pred_Control),
  accuracy(test_pred, truth = Diagnosis, .pred_class),
  brier_class(test_pred, truth = Diagnosis, .pred_Control)
) |>
  select(.metric, test = .estimate)

cv_metrics |> left_join(test_metrics, by = ".metric")
conf_mat(test_pred, truth = Diagnosis, estimate = .pred_class)
```

```{r, fig.width=5, fig.height=5}
roc_curve(test_pred, truth = Diagnosis, .pred_Control) |>
  autoplot() +
  labs(title = "PLS-DA test-set ROC (Control vs Breast cancer)",
       subtitle = "num_comp = 2, 27 training-selected compounds")
```

The final model generalizes well: **test-set ROC AUC 0.95, accuracy 0.96,
Brier score 0.13**, versus the null baseline's AUC of 0.50 and accuracy
0.64. Test metrics closely track the cross-validation estimates (CV AUC
0.985), indicating little overfitting. On the 53 held-out samples, all 34
cancer cases were correctly classified (perfect sensitivity) and 17 of 19
controls were correct (2 controls misclassified as cancer).

**Caveats.** (1) The held-out test evaluation is honest with respect to the
*test* set -- it played no role in feature selection or fitting -- but the
cross-validation AUC is mildly optimistic because feature selection was done
once on the whole training set rather than re-run inside each CV fold; the
test-set number is the estimate to trust. (2) This classifies Control vs.
Cancer, the signal we established is real; it does **not** predict stage,
consistent with every earlier result. (3) With only 19 controls in the test
set, the specificity estimate (17/19 = 0.89) has a wide confidence interval,
so the two control misclassifications shouldn't be over-interpreted.

## Stage-specific models: predicting each Cancer Stage vs. Control

Every analysis above (ANOVA/Tukey, sample-sample correlation, PCA) shows the
same pattern: each cancer Stage separates from Control, but Stages 1-4 do not
separate well from *each other*. A single 5-way classifier (Control vs.
Stage 1 vs. 2 vs. 3 vs. 4) would be fighting that structure. Instead we build
**four independent binary PLS-DA models** -- Stage 1 vs Control, Stage 2 vs
Control, Stage 3 vs Control, Stage 4 vs Control -- each trained and evaluated
only on Control samples plus that one cancer stage, using Healthy Control as
the shared negative class throughout.

Each model repeats the same leakage-free procedure as the Control-vs-Cancer
PLS-DA above: split into train/test first, then re-run ANOVA + BH selection
**using only that model's training samples** to pick predictors, then tune
a PLS-DA classifier's number of components. Folds are reduced from 10 to 5
because some per-stage training sets are small (Stage 1 has only 19 cancer
cases in total).

```{r}
library(tidymodels)
library(plsmod)
library(broom)
library(tibble)

fit_stage_vs_control <- function(stage_level, seed_split = 4127, seed_cv = 6183, seed_tune = 7321) {

  df_stage <- lcms_long_log |>
    filter(Stage %in% c("-", stage_level)) |>
    select(Compound, sample_id, log_abundance) |>
    pivot_wider(names_from = Compound, values_from = log_abundance) |>
    left_join(metadata_merged |> select(sample_id, Stage) |> distinct(), by = "sample_id") |>
    mutate(Stage = factor(ifelse(Stage == "-", "Control", paste0("Stage", stage_level)),
                           levels = c("Control", paste0("Stage", stage_level)))) |>
    column_to_rownames("sample_id")

  set.seed(seed_split)
  split <- initial_split(df_stage, strata = Stage)
  train <- training(split)
  test  <- testing(split)

  # Re-select significant compounds using TRAINING DATA ONLY for this stage's contrast
  train_ids <- rownames(train)
  anova_train <- lcms_long_log |>
    filter(sample_id %in% train_ids) |>
    mutate(Stage = droplevels(Stage)) |>
    group_by(Compound) |>
    nest() |>
    mutate(
      model = map(data, ~ aov(log_abundance ~ Stage, data = .x)),
      tidy_model = map(model, broom::tidy)
    ) |>
    select(Compound, tidy_model) |>
    unnest(tidy_model) |>
    filter(term == "Stage") |>
    ungroup() |>
    mutate(p_adj_BH = p.adjust(p.value, method = "BH"))

  predictor_cols <- anova_train |> filter(p_adj_BH < 0.05) |> pull(Compound)
  # Fallback to nominal p < .05 if BH leaves nothing (guards the smallest stages)
  if (length(predictor_cols) == 0) {
    predictor_cols <- anova_train |> filter(p.value < 0.05) |> pull(Compound)
  }

  train_final <- train[, c(predictor_cols, "Stage")]
  test_final  <- test[, c(predictor_cols, "Stage")]

  set.seed(seed_cv)
  folds <- vfold_cv(train_final, v = 5, strata = Stage)
  metrics_class <- metric_set(roc_auc, accuracy, brier_class)
  max_comp <- min(10, length(predictor_cols))

  pls_wf <- workflow() |>
    add_recipe(
      recipe(Stage ~ ., data = train_final) |>
        step_impute_median(all_numeric_predictors()) |>
        step_normalize(all_numeric_predictors())
    ) |>
    add_model(pls(num_comp = tune()) |> set_engine("mixOmics") |> set_mode("classification"))

  set.seed(seed_tune)
  pls_tune <- tune_grid(
    pls_wf, resamples = folds,
    grid = tibble(num_comp = 1:max_comp),
    metrics = metrics_class
  )

  best_comp <- collect_metrics(pls_tune) |>
    filter(.metric == "roc_auc") |>
    slice_max(mean, n = 1, with_ties = FALSE) |>
    pull(num_comp)

  pls_final_wf <- finalize_workflow(pls_wf, tibble(num_comp = best_comp))
  pls_fit <- fit(pls_final_wf, data = train_final)

  test_pred <- test_final |>
    bind_cols(predict(pls_fit, test_final, type = "prob")) |>
    bind_cols(predict(pls_fit, test_final, type = "class"))

  stage_label <- paste0("Stage", stage_level)
  test_metrics <- bind_rows(
    roc_auc(test_pred, truth = Stage, .pred_Control),
    accuracy(test_pred, truth = Stage, .pred_class),
    brier_class(test_pred, truth = Stage, .pred_Control)
  ) |>
    mutate(stage = stage_label)

  list(
    stage = stage_label,
    n_train = nrow(train_final), n_test = nrow(test_final),
    n_predictors = length(predictor_cols), predictors = predictor_cols,
    best_comp = best_comp, test_metrics = test_metrics, test_pred = test_pred,
    conf_mat = conf_mat(test_pred, truth = Stage, estimate = .pred_class)
  )
}

stage_results <- map(c("1", "2", "3", "4"), fit_stage_vs_control)
names(stage_results) <- paste0("Stage", c("1", "2", "3", "4"))
```

### Test-set performance by stage

```{r}
map_dfr(stage_results, ~ tibble(
  stage = .x$stage, n_train = .x$n_train, n_test = .x$n_test,
  n_predictors = .x$n_predictors, num_comp = .x$best_comp
))

map_dfr(stage_results, ~ .x$test_metrics) |>
  select(stage, .metric, .estimate) |>
  pivot_wider(names_from = .metric, values_from = .estimate)

walk(stage_results, ~ {
  cat("\n", .x$stage, "vs Control:\n")
  print(.x$conf_mat)
})
```

All four models beat the Control-vs-Cancer null baseline (AUC 0.50) by a wide
margin, but performance is not uniform: **Stage 1** (24 predictors, 4
components) reaches AUC 0.99 / accuracy 0.92 (22/24, with one misclassification
in each direction on a test set of only 5 Stage 1 cases); **Stage 2** (18
predictors, 3 components) is the weakest of the four at AUC 0.87 / accuracy
0.88 (28/32), missing 4 of 13 Stage 2 test cases as false negatives while
Control specificity stays perfect; **Stage 3** (14 predictors, 5 components)
achieves perfect test-set separation (AUC 1.00 / accuracy 1.00, 31/31); and
**Stage 4** (19 predictors, 2 components) reaches AUC 1.00 / accuracy 0.92
(22/24), correctly classifying all 5 Stage 4 test cases (perfect sensitivity)
but misclassifying 2 of 19 controls as Stage 4.

### ROC curves

```{r, fig.width=8, fig.height=7}
roc_data <- map_dfr(stage_results, function(x) {
  roc_curve(x$test_pred, truth = Stage, .pred_Control) |> mutate(stage = x$stage)
})

ggplot(roc_data, aes(x = 1 - specificity, y = sensitivity)) +
  geom_path() +
  geom_abline(lty = 3, color = "grey60") +
  facet_wrap(~stage) +
  coord_equal() +
  labs(title = "Stage-specific PLS-DA test-set ROC curves (each Stage vs Control)")
```

### Which compounds recur across stage-specific models?

```{r}
predictor_sets <- map(stage_results, "predictors")

predictor_overlap <- tibble(Compound = unique(unlist(predictor_sets))) |>
  mutate(
    Stage1 = Compound %in% predictor_sets$Stage1,
    Stage2 = Compound %in% predictor_sets$Stage2,
    Stage3 = Compound %in% predictor_sets$Stage3,
    Stage4 = Compound %in% predictor_sets$Stage4,
    n_stages = Stage1 + Stage2 + Stage3 + Stage4
  ) |>
  arrange(desc(n_stages))

predictor_overlap |> filter(n_stages >= 3)
```

Four compounds -- **Glutamine, Glycerophosphocholine, Pentosidine, and
Sphingosine 1-phosphate** -- are selected as significant predictors in
*every* stage-specific model. These are the same compounds flagged earlier as
top PC2 loadings driving the global Control-vs-Cancer separation, which is a
useful consistency check: the signal identified independently at every stage
converges on the same small set of "always-on" Control-vs-Cancer markers,
on top of a larger set of stage-specific compounds that vary from model to
model.

**Caveats.** (1) Each stage model is trained and evaluated independently; the
four classifiers were never trained to distinguish stages from one another,
so a genuinely new sample could in principle score "positive" under more than
one stage model at once -- these are four separate Stage-vs-Control screens,
not a single mutually-exclusive multi-way classifier. (2) Per-stage test sets
are small, especially for Stage 1 and Stage 4 (5 cancer cases each in the
test set); Stage 2 and Stage 3 have more test cases (13 and 12 respectively)
and give more stable estimates. (3) As with the global Control-vs-Cancer
model, `num_comp` was tuned once per stage rather than re-tuned inside each
CV fold, so cross-validation metrics would be mildly optimistic -- the
held-out test metrics reported above are the ones to trust. (4) Stage 2 shows
the weakest separation from Control (AUC 0.87 vs. ~0.99-1.00 for the other
three stages) despite having the largest cancer sample size of the four --
worth flagging as a stage that may need more samples or additional
predictors to resolve confidently, rather than concluding it is inherently
less metabolically distinct from Control.



## Receptor data

```{r}
receptor <- metadata_csv |>
  transmute(
    sample_id = `Sample name`,
    Diagnosis,
    ER  = case_when(ER == "1" ~ "ER+",  ER == "-" ~ "ER-",  TRUE ~ NA_character_),
    PR  = case_when(PR == "1" ~ "PR+",  PR == "-" ~ "PR-",  TRUE ~ NA_character_),
    HER2 = case_when(`HER-2 neu` == "1" ~ "HER2+", `HER-2 neu` == "-" ~ "HER2-", TRUE ~ NA_character_)
  ) |>
  filter(Diagnosis == "Breast cancer")

nrow(receptor)
```


```{r}
receptor |> count(ER)
receptor |> count(PR)
receptor |> count(HER2)
```

```{r}
cancer_ids <- receptor$sample_id
lw_cancer <- log_wide[, cancer_ids]
lw_cancer_imp <- t(apply(lw_cancer, 1, function(x) { x[is.na(x)] <- median(x, na.rm = TRUE); x }))

pca_cancer <- prcomp(t(lw_cancer_imp), scale. = TRUE)
vp1 <- round(summary(pca_cancer)$importance[2, "PC1"] * 100, 1)
vp2 <- round(summary(pca_cancer)$importance[2, "PC2"] * 100, 1)

scores_cancer <- as.data.frame(pca_cancer$x[, 1:2]) |>
  rownames_to_column("sample_id") |>
  left_join(receptor, by = "sample_id")

mk <- function(colvar) {
  d <- scores_cancer |> filter(!is.na(.data[[colvar]]))
  ggplot(d, aes(PC1, PC2, color = .data[[colvar]])) +
    geom_point(alpha = 0.8) +
    labs(title = colvar, x = paste0("PC1 (", vp1, "%)"), y = paste0("PC2 (", vp2, "%)"), color = NULL)
}

mk("ER") | mk("PR") | mk("HER2")
```

No gross separation by ER, PR, or HER-2 status appears in the top two principal components — the groups are thoroughly intermixed in all three panels. But I'd be cautious reading too much into this: PC1/PC2 capture only 23.6% of the variance across all 99 compounds, and recall the Control-vs-Cancer signal itself was invisible in the full-compound PCA and only emerged once we restricted to the significant compounds and looked at PC2. So this plot argues against a large, global receptor effect, but it does not rule out differences in individual compounds.


## Adding clinical covariates: receptor status, Age, and BMI

The receptor panels above test ER/PR/HER2 one at a time and don't account for
Age or BMI, both of which can independently shift metabolite levels and so
could confound a raw receptor-status comparison. Here we (1) collapse
ER/PR/HER2 into a single, better-powered **Receptor+ vs Triple-negative**
contrast, and (2) fit a covariate-adjusted linear regression per compound --
`log_abundance ~ HR_status + Age + BMI` -- so the receptor-status effect is
estimated *after* controlling for Age and BMI.

`metadata_merged` already carries the raw `ER`, `PR`, `HER-2 neu`,
`Age (BOD-OD)` (age at blood draw -- the biologically relevant age here, as
opposed to `Age (now)`, which is a data-collection-year artifact for Control
rows) and `BMI` columns; they were never dropped by the earlier
`select(-ends_with(...))` step. `lcms_long_log` inherits them too, so before
joining our derived covariates we select down to just `Compound`,
`sample_id`, `log_abundance` -- otherwise the join produces `BMI.x`/`BMI.y`-style
duplicates instead of a single usable `BMI` column.

```{r}
receptor_full <- metadata_merged |>
  filter(Diagnosis == "Breast cancer") |>
  transmute(
    sample_id,
    ER   = case_when(ER == "1" ~ "ER+",  ER == "-" ~ "ER-",  TRUE ~ NA_character_),
    PR   = case_when(PR == "1" ~ "PR+",  PR == "-" ~ "PR-",  TRUE ~ NA_character_),
    HER2 = case_when(`HER-2 neu` == "1" ~ "HER2+", `HER-2 neu` == "-" ~ "HER2-", TRUE ~ NA_character_),
    Age  = `Age (BOD-OD)`,
    BMI
  ) |>
  mutate(
    HR_status = case_when(
      ER == "ER+" | PR == "PR+" | HER2 == "HER2+" ~ "Receptor+",
      ER == "ER-" & PR == "PR-" & HER2 == "HER2-" ~ "Triple-negative",
      TRUE ~ NA_character_
    ),
    HR_status = factor(HR_status, levels = c("Receptor+", "Triple-negative"))
  ) |>
  filter(!is.na(HR_status), !is.na(Age), !is.na(BMI))

nrow(receptor_full)
receptor_full |> count(HR_status)

lcms_receptor <- lcms_long_log |>
  select(Compound, sample_id, log_abundance) |>
  inner_join(receptor_full, by = "sample_id")
```

119 of the 135 cancer samples have complete ER/PR/HER2/Age/BMI data (16
excluded: 10 missing at least one receptor call, 10 missing BMI, with some
overlap), splitting 95 Receptor+ vs 24 Triple-negative -- still imbalanced,
but a cleaner two-group contrast than three separate binary receptor calls.

### Linear regression: a single compound worked example

```{r}
glutamine_fit <- lm(log_abundance ~ HR_status + Age + BMI,
                     data = lcms_receptor |> filter(Compound == "Glutamine"))
summary(glutamine_fit)
```

For Glutamine, none of the three covariates reach significance individually
(HR status p = .25, Age p = .13, BMI p = .32), and the full model explains
only 5% of variance (adjusted R² = 0.028) -- Glutamine's earlier
Control-vs-Cancer signal doesn't extend to a within-cancer receptor/age/BMI
effect.

### Systematic per-compound regression, BH-corrected

```{r}
lm_results <- lcms_receptor |>
  group_by(Compound) |>
  nest() |>
  mutate(
    model = map(data, ~ lm(log_abundance ~ HR_status + Age + BMI, data = .x)),
    tidy_model = map(model, broom::tidy)
  ) |>
  select(Compound, tidy_model) |>
  unnest(tidy_model) |>
  ungroup()

hr_effect <- lm_results |>
  filter(term == "HR_statusTriple-negative") |>
  mutate(p_adj_BH = p.adjust(p.value, method = "BH")) |>
  arrange(p_adj_BH)

age_effect <- lm_results |>
  filter(term == "Age") |>
  mutate(p_adj_BH = p.adjust(p.value, method = "BH")) |>
  arrange(p_adj_BH)

bmi_effect <- lm_results |>
  filter(term == "BMI") |>
  mutate(p_adj_BH = p.adjust(p.value, method = "BH")) |>
  arrange(p_adj_BH)

cat("HR status -- significant (BH < .05):", sum(hr_effect$p_adj_BH < 0.05), "of 99\n")
cat("Age       -- significant (BH < .05):", sum(age_effect$p_adj_BH < 0.05), "of 99\n")
cat("BMI       -- significant (BH < .05):", sum(bmi_effect$p_adj_BH < 0.05), "of 99\n")

age_effect |> select(Compound, estimate, p.value, p_adj_BH) |> head(9)
```

**Receptor status: 0 of 99 compounds** remain significant after BH
correction -- consistent with the PCA panels above showing no gross
receptor-status separation, and now confirmed at the individual-compound
level even after adjusting for Age and BMI. **BMI: 0 of 99** compounds
survive correction either (a handful have nominal p < .01, e.g.
3-Indolepropionic acid, Phenyllactic acid, Succinyladenosine, but none
withstand testing across 99 compounds). **Age is the one covariate with a
real signal: 9 of 99 compounds** remain significant after BH correction,
led by Quinic acid, *trans*-Hexadec-2-enoyl carnitine, Tetradecanoylcarnitine,
Androstenedione, and Glycolaldehyde (all p_adj < .01) -- an age-related
metabolite signature independent of receptor status, worth keeping in mind
as a potential confounder in any future model that doesn't explicitly
adjust for it.

### Repeating the receptor PCA with the collapsed HR+ / Triple-negative contrast

```{r, fig.width=5, fig.height=4}
scores_cancer_hr <- scores_cancer |>
  left_join(receptor_full |> select(sample_id, HR_status), by = "sample_id")

ggplot(scores_cancer_hr |> filter(!is.na(HR_status)), aes(PC1, PC2, color = HR_status)) +
  geom_point(alpha = 0.8) +
  labs(title = "HR status (Receptor+ vs Triple-negative)",
       x = paste0("PC1 (", vp1, "%)"), y = paste0("PC2 (", vp2, "%)"), color = NULL)
```

As with the three-way ER/PR/HER2 split, the collapsed HR+/Triple-negative
groups are still thoroughly intermixed on PC1/PC2 -- the better-powered
contrast doesn't reveal a global receptor-status structure the three-way
split was missing. Combined with the per-compound regression above, receptor
status looks like it has, at most, a small, compound-specific effect on this
platform rather than a broad metabolic signature -- unlike the clear
Control-vs-Cancer separation established earlier in this document.

**Caveats.** (1) Three covariate terms were tested per compound (HR status,
Age, BMI); each was BH-corrected across the 99 compounds independently for
that term, not jointly across all ~297 tests, matching how each earlier
single-factor analysis in this document was corrected. (2) The
Triple-negative group is small (n = 24) relative to Receptor+ (n = 95), so
the HR-status term has limited power to detect anything but a fairly large
effect -- absence of significance here is not strong evidence of *no* effect,
just of no *detectable* one at this sample size. (3) `Age (BOD-OD)` (age at
blood draw) was used rather than `Age (now)`, which is not usable for this
purpose (it is populated with a collection year, not an age, for Control
rows, and is a different, less relevant reference point even for cancer
rows).
